results.title: Quantization as Survival Analysis: Discrete-Time Proportional Hazards Models for Bit-Width Collapse Prediction
results.abstract: Post-training quantization of large language models (LLMs) requires careful allocation of bit-widths across heterogeneous architectural components. Existing sensitivity metrics rely on gradient norms, Hessian traces, or activation ranges, all of which are computed at a fixed bit-width and do not account for the sequential, multi-stage nature of progressive compression. We propose to reframe quantization fragility as a survival problem: each transformer block is treated as a unit subject to a failure event—a critical performance collapse—as bit-width decreases from 16 to 2 bits through an ordered schedule <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\mathcal {B} = \langle 16,12,8,6,5,4,3,2 \rangle $ </tex-math></inline-formula>. We build a discrete-time interval-censored survival dataset from one-at-a-time block quantization experiments and fit a discrete-time proportional hazards model via complementary log-log (cloglog) regression. The resulting hazard ratios provide statistically grounded, architecture- aware predictors of collapse timing. We demonstrate that depth-normalised position (HR = 8.54, <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$p \lt 10^{-4}$ </tex-math></inline-formula>) and weight variance-to-mean ratio (HR = 3.98, <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$p \lt 10^{-3}$ </tex-math></inline-formula>) are the dominant structural predictors of quantization vulnerability, while attention head density provides a protective effect (HR = 0.40, <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$p \lt 0.002$ </tex-math></inline-formula>). A survival-driven mixed-precision allocation (SurvAlloc) derived from these hazard ratios outperforms uniform INT4 quantization by + 1.2–+ 2.7 MMLU points at a comparable memory footprint across TinyLlama-1.1B, Llama-2-7B, OPT-6.7B, and Mistral-7B. The concordance index reaches <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$0.81~[{0.76, 0.86}]$ </tex-math></inline-formula>, confirmed non-random by a Monte Carlo permutation test (<inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$p \lt 10^{-4}$ </tex-math></inline-formula>).
